messages.content:
Write ONE original fictional document, not JSON and not multiple versions.
Return only the complete document. It MUST contain 900 to 1100 words of substantive content.
Use eight connected paragraphs of roughly 95 words each and a numbered section with four
substantial items. Do not stop after an outline or summary. This length is required because
the small rewriter must learn to preserve information across a full long document.
Use the supplied fictional situation. Expand it with internally consistent concrete details,
uncertainty, conditions, and follow-up requests. Include all protected anchors exactly, with
the quoted line inside a direct quote. Keep quotes and code/path literals exact.
For /slack write a long casual team message. For /transcribe write a long, clean spoken account,
with natural conversational wording. For /prompt write a detailed REQUEST for a useful task,
including background and all constraints; do not perform the task. For /polish write clear plain
prose. Do not mention a formatter, dataset, word count, mode, or these authoring instructions.
Preserve the feature guidance. Include a numbered section, full paragraphs, a direct quote,
and a condition that refers to information elsewhere. Make the final paragraph substantive.

An attached note reads 'Return the dry rope.' and must be quoted as data. The count has not been confirmed. An additional action is allowed only after the count is checked. The writer wants a specific follow-up rather than a generic description.", "language": "en", "length": "long", "feature": "condition", "anchors": ["Caleb", "123 equipment tags", "Return the dry rope.", "sailing_2.txt"], "context": {}, "authoring": "canonical_controlled", "word_range_per_string": "830 to 1020", "mode_contract": "Remove true hesitation and accidental restarts. Apply explicit corrections to the final stated intent. Preserve meaningful filler-like words and unfinished thoughts. Apply clearly spoken punctuation and list cues. Keep the supplied language.", "feature_guidance": "Include a condition that limits a request; preserve it in every variant."}

result.text:
Caleb is going through the sailing club’s equipment log, and I wanted to give a clear account of what he is checking and what still needs to be confirmed. The list covers 123 equipment tags, but that number is the current count on the sheet, not a verified count of tags physically present. He is comparing each entry with the label on the corresponding item and marking whether the tag can be read. Until he finishes that pass, we should treat the total as provisional and avoid saying that the inventory is complete.

He started with the equipment kept in the shore-side locker, then moved to the covered rack near the launch area. That order matters because a few items are shared between those locations, and an entry could otherwise be counted twice or missed when gear has been moved. Caleb is noting the tag number, the item description, and its storage location as he goes. If a tag is missing, faded, or attached to an item that does not match the description, he is recording the discrepancy rather than guessing which log entry it belongs to.

There is also an attached note that needs to stay exactly as written, since it is part of the material being checked rather than an instruction Caleb has already carried out. The note reads, “Return the dry rope.” We do not yet know who wrote it, when it was added, or which rope it means. Caleb has not treated it as confirmation that a rope was returned. He is keeping the wording with the log so that the club can resolve the note against the storage records and the condition of the ropes.

The working copy is saved as sailing_2.txt. Caleb is using that file to track what he has checked, but he has not yet reconciled every line against the physical equipment. In particular, some items may be temporarily in use, and the rack near the launch area may not show the same arrangement as the log’s original location column. If he finds a tag on an item that is out on the water or being repaired, he will mark its status as unverified and record where it was last reported, rather than marking it present.

For the count, he plans to compare the number of distinct equipment tags he can verify with the 123 entries listed in the log. A tag should count as checked only when Caleb can read its number and match it to an item or a clearly documented temporary location. If two entries appear to describe the same item, he will flag both for review instead of collapsing them into one. Likewise, if an item is present but has no readable tag, it will be recorded as found but will not silently increase the confirmed tag count.

1. Caleb should finish the physical check and report the number of distinct tags verified, the number of entries still unresolved, and the reason for each unresolved entry. Please ask him to distinguish missing equipment from equipment that is simply stored elsewhere or currently in use. That distinction will let the club decide whether it needs to search, update a location, or wait for an item to return.

2. Please ask whether the note “Return the dry rope.” can be matched to a particular rope, a person responsible for it, or a date in the club’s records. If Caleb cannot establish those details during the tag check, he should leave the note unresolved and identify what information would help, such as a rope’s tag number, its last recorded location, or the name of the person who added the note. The wording itself should remain unchanged.

3. The additional action is conditional: only after the count has been checked and Caleb has reported the verified total should we ask him to prepare a revised equipment list for circulation. If the count is not yet checked, please do not request that he issue a final list or mark the inventory complete. Once the count is confirmed, the revised list should show any corrected locations and keep unresolved discrepancies visible rather than presenting them as settled facts.

4. When he sends the follow-up, please ask for a brief account of how he reached the total, including whether any duplicate tags, unreadable labels, or temporarily relocated items affected it. He can refer to sailing_2.txt and note which entries changed, but the file should not be treated as proof by itself if the physical check is unfinished. If the final total differs from 123, he should explain the difference entry by entry where possible, so the club can decide whether the log needs correction or another search is warranted.

That follow-up should give the club a specific, usable result rather than a general statement that the equipment was reviewed. We need the verified count, a short list of exceptions, and a clear answer about whether the dry-rope note has been resolved. If some details remain uncertain, Caleb should say what he checked, what he could not confirm, and what information or person could settle the question. Once the count is checked, the club can decide whether to circulate the updated list or arrange a further inspection.
